summary: Reserves two blocks of Autonomous System numbers for use in examples in RFCs, books, and other documentation, to avoid confusion with real deployed networks. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5398 reserves two ranges of Autonomous System numbers for examples in RFCs, books, and other documentation. Using these numbers helps distinguish examples from AS numbers used by deployed networks.

can i use any as number for examples
as number ranges for test networks
subtitle: Autonomous System number ranges reserved for examples in documentation.

tldr.problem: Using operational Autonomous System numbers in examples can confuse readers and may cause conflicts if the examples are copied into real configurations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reserves two blocks of 16 AS numbers for documentation: one in the 16-bit range and one in the 32-bit range.
tldr.outcome: Documentation can use the reserved blocks to distinguish example numbers from public or private-use AS numbers. BGP configurations should not peer with these reserved ASNs.

today: RFC 5398 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. It reserves two AS number blocks for documentation and examples.

sections.title: Why Documentation Needs Reserved AS Numbers
sections.content:
An Autonomous System number (ASN) identifies an autonomous system in routing. RFC 5398 reserves numbers for examples in RFCs, books, and similar documentation to reduce confusion between examples and deployed systems.

The memo notes that literal use of documented IPv4 examples in production has caused address and routing conflicts. It also says private-use AS numbers are unsuitable for many examples because they already have a role in deployed networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Examples need numbers that readers can recognize as examples. This RFC reserves AS numbers so documentation does not use numbers intended for real networks.

sections.title: The Reserved Number Ranges
sections.content:
The RFC reserves two contiguous blocks, each containing 16 AS numbers. The first is 64496 through 64511, within the range expressible as a 16-bit AS number. The second is 65536 through 65551, within the range that requires 32-bit AS numbers.

The two blocks allow documentation to describe examples involving both 16-bit and 32-bit AS number values. The memo states that IANA reserved these ranges and recorded them in the IANA AS Number Registry.
sections.plainLanguage: One reserved range is for 16-bit AS numbers, and the other is for 32-bit AS numbers. Each range contains 16 numbers for examples.

sections.title: How Routers Should Treat the Ranges
sections.content:
The memo says BGP operational configurations should not peer with neighboring autonomous systems numbered from either reserved block. Reserving the blocks is intended to reduce conflicts when documentation examples are copied into production routing configurations.

The security considerations state that AS number reservations have no direct impact on Internet infrastructure security.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP configurations should not establish peerings with these reserved example numbers. The RFC says the reservations do not directly affect Internet infrastructure security.
